Charted a long southern coast, some of which was later removed and some of which was not.
The first sustained survey in the dataset, and the expedition that sailed across positions Wilkes had charted as land.
Frank Worsley navigated Endurance and the James Caird; the navigation, not the endurance, is what Act VIII is about.
A survey voyage chartered after Smith's earlier sighting of the South Shetlands. One of the three parties advanced as first to see the mainland.
A sealing voyage, which is why its record is thinner than the naval ones and why the priority argument around it turns on what a commercial log counts as.
Reached an exceptional southern latitude in open water, in a season whose ice conditions were not typical. The sea later named for him is the one Endurance is beset in.
A pendulum and magnetic survey rather than a discovery voyage, and named on both cumulative ice charts. Included because Act VII is about what gets compiled, not about who saw land.
A commercial voyage that produced coast, which is the combination the discovery historiography handles worst.
Named on both ice charts for the 1839 season.
One of three expeditions working the same coast in the 1840 season. The overlap is the point: three national accounts of weeks that each claims differently.
The first vessel to winter in the Antarctic pack, and a candidate for Act VII only if its survey work can be shown on a chart.
